title: Architecture-dependent Effects of Trade-offs on Evolutionary Navigability and Epistasis
summary: The structure of the genotype-phenotype map plays a central role in determining how populations move through fitness landscapes, yet less is known about how this structure interacts with environmental constraints and fitness trade-offs. Here, we study evolution on a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map in which binary genotypes are transformed through successive feed-forward layers before being evaluated by phenotype-level fitness functions. We explicitly model the phenotype to fitness transformation in order to compare an emergent trade-off fitness with a no-trade-off control. We explore different map architecture as models of more and less complex genotype-phenotype relationships by tuning the genotype length and number of layers. We find that ruggedness and navigability have a complex, architecture-dependent relationship. Landscapes with few local maxima can still have low navigability for wide and shallow maps, and navigability is high even at mean values of ruggedness for wide and deep maps. Trade-offs increase navigability in wide and shallow maps, while their effect is muted in other architectures. The effect of trade-offs on epistasis depends on evolutionary history. While trade-offs change which mutational neighborhoods are sampled by evolution, the background degree of epistatic interactions is set by map architecture. Finally, we use our framework to investigate micro-evolution of high-fitness populations and show that temporal covariance in allele-frequency changes can arise from the internal structure of a rugged genotype-phenotype map, producing signatures that resemble short-term alternating selection.

AI.tldr: This paper studies evolution on a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map with feed-forward layers, examining how map architecture (genotype length and layer number) interacts with fitness trade-offs to shape landscape ruggedness, navigability, epistasis, and evolutionary dynamics.
AI.motivation: While the structure of the genotype-phenotype map is known to govern how populations traverse fitness landscapes, less is understood about how this structure interacts with environmental constraints and fitness trade-offs. The authors aim to fill this gap by explicitly modeling phenotype-to-fitness transformations to compare trade-off and no-trade-off scenarios.
AI.method: The authors construct a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map where binary genotypes pass through successive feed-forward layers before being evaluated by phenotype-level fitness functions. They tune map complexity by varying genotype length and number of layers, and compare architectures under an emergent trade-off fitness function versus a no-trade-off control.
AI.result: Ruggedness and navigability show a complex, architecture-dependent relationship: wide and shallow maps can have few local maxima yet low navigability, while wide and deep maps achieve high navigability even at mean ruggedness. Trade-offs increase navigability only in wide and shallow maps. The effect of trade-offs on epistasis is history-dependent, while background epistasis is set by architecture. In micro-evolution of high-fitness populations, internal structure of rugged maps can generate temporal covariance in allele-frequency changes resembling short-term alternating selection.
AI.conclusion: Map architecture sets the fundamental context for evolutionary dynamics, with trade-offs modulating navigability only under certain architectures. The framework also reveals that apparent signatures of alternating selection in allele-frequency data can emerge purely from the internal structure of a rugged genotype-phenotype map, without actual environmental fluctuations.

title: SurfSpec: Enhancing Off-Target-Agnostic Specificity by Bounding Pocket-Ligand Geometric Mismatch
summary: Lead optimization in structure-based drug design aims to improve target binding while avoiding unintended interactions with off-target pockets. However, existing affinity-driven methods do not explicitly control specificity, whereas current specificity-aware approaches commonly require prior knowledge of off-target structures. We address off-target-agnostic specificity-aware lead optimization by analyzing the geometric mismatch between a ligand and the target pocket. We provide a conservative specificity lower bound for geometrically separated off-targets without requiring access to off-target structures. By metricizing pocket--ligand mismatch, the triangle inequality shows that reducing target--ligand mismatch improves a conservative lower bound on mismatch to a separated off-target class, which can be translated into a specificity lower bound through an empirical geometry--affinity calibration. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce SurfSpec, an off-target-agnostic lead optimization framework that iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. SurfSpec alternates between linker generation toward selected target-surface patches, which provides geometric pseudo-labels, and refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior, which restores these pseudo-labels into valid ligands. On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch and outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, while maintaining competitive target-affinity improvement.

AI.tldr: SurfSpec is an off-target-agnostic lead optimization framework that improves ligand specificity by growing molecules toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface, reducing geometric mismatch with the target pocket without requiring knowledge of off-target structures.
AI.motivation: Existing affinity-driven lead optimization methods do not explicitly control specificity (avoiding off-target binding), while current specificity-aware approaches require prior knowledge of off-target structures. The authors aim to address off-target-agnostic specificity-aware lead optimization by analyzing geometric mismatch between a ligand and the target pocket.
AI.method: The paper derives a conservative specificity lower bound for geometrically separated off-targets using the triangle inequality on metricized pocket-ligand mismatch, without needing off-target structures. This bound is translated into specificity via an empirical geometry-affinity calibration. Building on this analysis, SurfSpec iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface, alternating between linker generation toward selected target-surface patches (providing geometric pseudo-labels) and refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior to convert pseudo-labels into valid ligands.
AI.result: On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch and outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, while maintaining competitive target-affinity improvement.
AI.conclusion: SurfSpec demonstrates that off-target-agnostic specificity-aware lead optimization is achievable by exploiting geometric mismatch with the target pocket as a proxy for specificity, providing a theoretical foundation via the triangle inequality and empirically validating this approach on standard benchmarks.

title: Sparse concept attribution for histomorphological hypothesis generation from whole-slide classifiers
summary: Histology images contain rich morphological information and can provide insights into pathological processes. However, deriving hypotheses relating morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by a manual image interpretation step. Here, we demonstrate that this process can be automated through interpretable deep learning. We present SCOPE, a method to interpret slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision--language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. To measure whether such explanations recover known morphology, we introduce MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions. On this benchmark, dense concept attribution is indistinguishable from a random baseline, whereas sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology; decomposing the pooled slide embedding reaches similar explanation correctness at a fraction of the computational cost. Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can thus generate morphological hypotheses at scale, for expert validation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SCOPE, a method that automates the interpretation of histology whole-slide classifiers by using pathology-specific vision-language models combined with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. It introduces MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions, showing that sparse attribution recovers known morphology while dense attribution performs no better than random, and that decomposing pooled slide embeddings achieves comparable results at lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Deriving hypotheses linking morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes in histology images is bottlenecked by manual image interpretation. The authors aim to automate this process through interpretable deep learning.
AI.method: SCOPE interprets slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision-language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. The authors evaluate using MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions, comparing dense vs. sparse attribution and pooled slide embedding decomposition.
AI.result: On MorphoRecoveryBench, dense concept attribution is indistinguishable from a random baseline, whereas sparse attribution substantially recovers known morphology. Decomposing the pooled slide embedding achieves similar explanation correctness at a fraction of the computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can generate morphological hypotheses at scale, providing a practical path for expert validation without manual image interpretation bottlenecks.

title: Advances in Machine Learning for Directed Evolution: A Five-Year Retrospective
summary: The last five-plus years have seen many protein engineering disciplines transformed by advances in machine learning (ML), but the same cannot be said for directed evolution. Reflecting on a previously co-authored perspective, I discuss why I believe this to be the case, arguing that a disconnect between the goals of machine-learning-assisted directed evolution (MLDE) researchers--"identify an optimal protein"--and the goals of directed evolution more broadly--"identify a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints"--is a principal culprit. As an example, I highlight how nearly all current MLDE methods neglect to account for the cost of DNA synthesis, resulting in strategies that have limited practical applicability regardless of the underlying models' capabilities. I close by discussing recent works that are exceptions to this overarching trend, and emphasize that the last five years of efforts in ML-assisted protein engineering and the prescribed reframe of MLDE objectives need not be mutually exclusive.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper argues that machine-learning-assisted directed evolution (MLDE) has underperformed relative to other ML-transformed protein engineering fields because researchers optimize for "identifying an optimal protein" rather than directed evolution's real-world goal of "identifying a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints." The author highlights how most MLDE methods ignore the cost of DNA synthesis, limiting practical applicability, and discusses recent exceptions that bridge this gap.
AI.motivation: Despite significant advances in ML for protein engineering over the past five years, directed evolution has not seen the same transformation. The author identifies a fundamental disconnect between MLDE researchers' optimization goals (finding optimal proteins) and the practical goals of directed evolution (finding sufficient proteins within real-world constraints like time and costs).
AI.method: This is a perspective/opinion essay, not an empirical study. It involves reflective analysis of the MLDE field, drawing on the author's previous co-authored perspective, arguing that neglecting real-world constraints (particularly DNA synthesis costs) in MLDE objective functions is a principal reason for limited practical impact.
AI.result: The author argues that nearly all current MLDE methods fail to account for DNA synthesis costs, making their strategies practically inapplicable regardless of model capability. Recent works are cited as exceptions to this trend.
AI.conclusion: Reframing MLDE objectives to align with directed evolution's practical constraints (sufficiency, resource limits) is necessary, but this reframing is complementary to—not mutually exclusive with—the past five years of ML-assisted protein engineering advances.

title: Enhancer-promoter proximity predicts transcriptional competence but not transcriptional output in the Drosophila brain
summary: How 3D genome architecture contributes to transcriptional specificity across neuronal cell types remains unclear. Here, we used multiplexed chromatin tracing to map chromatin architecture and cell identity at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain. We found that enhancer-promoter (E-P) proximity was increased in transcriptionally active compared with inactive neurons. Analysis of single traces revealed the existence of distinct proximal and distal E-P states, with active neurons enriched in the proximal state. However, this relationship broke down across active neuronal subtypes, where neither E-P proximity nor chromatin accessibility predicted transcriptional output. Thus, 3D genome organization distinguishes transcriptionally competent from inactive neuronal states without quantitatively specifying transcriptional output. Our findings support a model in which E-P proximity establishes a permissive structural state, while additional cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms tune transcriptional output.

AI.tldr: Using multiplexed chromatin tracing at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain, this study reveals that enhancer-promoter (E-P) proximity is increased in transcriptionally active versus inactive neurons, distinguishing active from inactive states. However, E-P proximity does not quantitatively predict transcriptional output across active neuronal subtypes, supporting a model where E-P proximity creates a permissive structural state while other regulatory mechanisms fine-tune transcription.
AI.motivation: To understand how 3D genome architecture contributes to cell-type-specific transcriptional regulation across neuronal subtypes, a question that remains unresolved.
AI.method: Multiplexed chromatin tracing was used to simultaneously map chromatin architecture and cell identity at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain.
AI.result: E-P proximity is increased in transcriptionally active neurons compared to inactive ones; active neurons are enriched in a proximal E-P state. However, across active neuronal subtypes, E-P proximity and chromatin accessibility do not predict transcriptional output.
AI.conclusion: 3D genome organization distinguishes transcriptionally competent from inactive neuronal states but does not quantitatively determine transcription. E-P proximity establishes a permissive structural state, while cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms modulate final transcriptional output.

title: An Integrative Computational Approach to Predict Viral Epitopes by Targeting the MHC-TCR Complexation
summary: T-cell immunity acts as a major defense system against controlling viral infections in vertebrates. During viral entry, innate immune cells degrade the viral proteins (antigens) and present them on their surface via Major Histocompatibility (MHC) proteins. T-cell receptors (TCRs) recognize these antigens/peptides presented by MHC (pMHC), initiating a T-cell mediated immune response. Despite its significance, the mechanism by which pMHC-TCR binding triggers T-cell activation remains unclear. In this study, we employed an integrative computational approach combining Bioinformatics, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, and Machine Learning (ML) to identify viral epitopes as potential vaccine candidates. We performed large-scale all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations on MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded into dendritic and T-cells, for which experimental immunogenicity data is available. One hundred fifty such systems are simulated for 1 μs each to capture the conformational and dynamical changes that underlie T-cell activation. Our ML model (DynamiT), trained on simulation-derived structural and dynamical features extracted from 2500 time points, revealed key determinants responsible for T-cell activation with an accuracy of 73.3%. Notably, we have identified the bending of the TCR transmembrane region, major dynamic motions of the TCRα constant region and the buried surface area at the pMHC and TCR interface as critical factors influencing immune response initiation. Our approach unravels the mechanism of T-cell mediated immune response and helps ML-guided screening of viral epitopes for vaccine development.

AI.tldr: This paper uses an integrative computational approach combining bioinformatics, all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations (150 MHC-peptide-TCR complexes simulated for 1 μs each), and a machine learning model (DynamiT) to uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying T-cell activation and identify viral epitopes as vaccine candidates. The ML model achieved 73.3% accuracy, identifying TCR transmembrane bending, TCRα constant region dynamics, and pMHC-TCR buried surface area as key determinants of immune response initiation.
AI.motivation: T-cell immunity is critical for controlling viral infections, yet the mechanistic details of how pMHC-TCR binding triggers T-cell activation remain unclear. Understanding this mechanism is essential for rational vaccine development and epitope screening.
AI.method: An integrative computational pipeline was employed combining: (1) bioinformatics for viral epitope identification, (2) large-scale all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations (150 MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded in dendritic and T-cell membranes, each simulated for 1 μs) with experimental immunogenicity data, and (3) a machine learning model (DynamiT) trained on simulation-derived structural and dynamical features from 2500 time points.
AI.result: The DynamiT ML model achieved 73.3% accuracy in predicting T-cell activation. Key determinants were identified: bending of the TCR transmembrane region, major dynamic motions of the TCRα constant region, and buried surface area at the pMHC-TCR interface were critical factors influencing immune response initiation.
AI.conclusion: This approach unravels the mechanistic basis of T-cell mediated immune responses and enables ML-guided screening of viral epitopes for vaccine development.

title: Coarse-Graining Agent-Based Models of Bacterial Infections
summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) provide a natural framework for representing cell-level rules and spatial heterogeneity in bacterial infections, but their computational cost limits their use for macroscopic tissue-scale simulations and broad parameter exploration. We derive a deterministic coarse-grained description for a class of bacterial-infection ABMs in which immune cells and extracellular bacteria diffuse, immune cells ingest nearby bacteria, and intracellular bacterial loads evolve through prescribed birth and clearance processes. The first coarse-grained model is a semidiscrete reaction--diffusion system that retains a discrete internal state for each immune-cell bacterial load while representing cell and bacterial populations by continuum concentration fields. The key technical step is the derivation of state-dependent effective ingestion rates from the microscopic ABM parameters: these rates are obtained by solving an auxiliary diffusion problem around a single bacterium and computing the flux of immune cells into the interaction region. We then take a continuum limit in the internal state variable, yielding a state-structured reaction--diffusion system in which intracellular dynamics appear as advection and diffusion in state space. Numerical comparisons with ensemble-averaged ABM simulations show close agreement in biologically motivated parameter regimes. The resulting framework preserves the rule-based structure of the ABM while producing PDE models that are substantially more tractable for large-scale simulation and parameter studies.

AI.tldr: The authors derive deterministic coarse-grained PDE models (a semidiscrete reaction-diffusion system and its continuum state-structured limit) from a class of agent-based models (ABMs) of bacterial infections, deriving state-dependent effective ingestion rates via auxiliary diffusion problems, and validate them against ensemble-averaged ABM simulations.
AI.motivation: ABMs naturally capture cell-level rules and spatial heterogeneity in bacterial infections, but their computational cost prohibits tissue-scale simulations and broad parameter exploration. There is a need for more tractable mathematical descriptions that retain the rule-based structure of ABMs.
AI.method: Two coarse-grained models are derived: (1) a semidiscrete reaction-diffusion system retaining discrete intracellular bacterial load states with continuum concentration fields for cell/bacterial populations, where effective ingestion rates are derived by solving an auxiliary diffusion problem around a single bacterium; (2) a continuum limit in the internal state variable leading to a state-structured reaction-diffusion system with advection and diffusion in state space.
AI.result: Numerical comparisons show close agreement between the derived PDE models and ensemble-averaged ABM simulations across biologically motivated parameter regimes, demonstrating the validity of the coarse-graining approach.
AI.conclusion: The framework bridges microscopic ABM rules and macroscopic PDE descriptions, producing substantially more tractable models for large-scale tissue simulations and parameter studies while preserving the rule-based structure of the original ABM.

title: Structural control over equilibrium silicon and oxygen isotopic fractionation: A first-principles density-functional theory study
summary: Isotopic fractionation factors for oxygen and silicon in selected silicates (quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, kaolinite) have been calculated using first-principles methods. Good agreement between theory and experiment is obtained in the case of oxygen. In the case of silicon, agreement and differences with existing estimates of equilibrium fractionation factors are discussed. The relationships between silicon fractionation factors and oxygen fractionation factors, silicate polymerization degree and chemical composition is studied. The previously stated relationship with the polymerization degree of the mineral is not confirmed. Nevertheless, our calculation suggests that silicon fractionation depends on the cationic content of the mineral, in a way similar to oxygen.  Oxygen fractionation properties could thus provide some insights on silicon fractionation behavior.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations of oxygen and silicon isotopic fractionation factors in five silicates (quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, kaolinite) show good theory-experiment agreement for oxygen and reveal that silicon fractionation depends on cationic content rather than polymerization degree.
AI.motivation: To determine equilibrium isotopic fractionation factors for oxygen and silicon in silicates, validate theoretical predictions against experiments, and understand what controls silicon fractionation behavior (previously proposed relationship with polymerization degree needed verification).
AI.method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory were performed for selected silicate minerals to compute reduced partition function ratios (beta factors) for both oxygen and silicon isotopes, using phonon calculations and the Bigeleisen-Mayer formalism for equilibrium isotopic fractionation.
AI.result: Oxygen fractionation factors agree well with experimental data. For silicon, differences from existing equilibrium fractionation estimates are discussed. The previously proposed relationship between silicon fractionation and degree of silicate polymerization is not confirmed. However, silicon fractionation does appear to depend on the cationic composition of the mineral, analogous to oxygen behavior.
AI.conclusion: Silicon isotopic fractionation in silicates is not controlled by polymerization degree as previously suggested, but correlates with cationic content similar to oxygen. Therefore, oxygen fractionation data may serve as a proxy to predict silicon fractionation behavior in silicate minerals.

title: The Identification of Biological Stains at Crime Scenes: A Promising Role for Proteomics and Machine Learning
summary: Forensic body fluid identification is crucial for reconstructing crime scene events. While DNA analysis provides individualization, it lacks information about the fluid's origin. We developed and evaluated three complementary proteomic approaches using LC-HRMS/MS to identify blood, saliva, semen, urine, and vaginal fluid, including complex mixtures. The first method utilized fluid-specific peptide biomarkers, achieving high accuracy for pure fluids. The second employed peptide abundance ratios, demonstrating effectiveness in body fluid mixtures. The third, a machine learning model using Classifier Chain Random Forest, achieved 100% accuracy for pure fluids and promising results for mixtures. Our results revealed the complementarity of different tests, with the peptide-specific biomarker and machine-learning approaches being the most robust. This study demonstrates the potential of proteomics for comprehensive body fluid identification, offering valuable tools for forensic investigations.

AI.tldr: This study developed and evaluated three complementary LC-HRMS/MS-based proteomic approaches (fluid-specific peptide biomarkers, peptide abundance ratios, and a Classifier Chain Random Forest machine learning model) to identify five body fluids (blood, saliva, semen, urine, vaginal fluid) including complex mixtures, with the machine learning model achieving 100% accuracy on pure fluids.
AI.motivation: Forensic body fluid identification is essential for crime scene reconstruction, but DNA analysis cannot determine the origin of biological fluids. There is a need for reliable methods to identify the specific type of body fluid present at crime scenes.
AI.method: Three complementary proteomic approaches were developed using LC-HRMS/MS: (1) fluid-specific peptide biomarker identification, (2) peptide abundance ratio analysis, and (3) a Classifier Chain Random Forest machine learning model. These were applied to identify blood, saliva, semen, urine, and vaginal fluid, including complex mixtures.
AI.result: The peptide-specific biomarker method achieved high accuracy for pure fluids, the peptide abundance ratio method was effective for mixtures, and the machine learning model achieved 100% accuracy for pure fluids with promising results for mixtures. The biomarker and machine-learning approaches were found to be the most robust.
AI.conclusion: Proteomics demonstrates strong potential for comprehensive body fluid identification, complementing DNA analysis in forensic investigations by providing reliable tools for determining the origin of biological evidence.

title: Modeling Tissue Detachment and Rupture Using an Extended Vertex Model with T2-inverse Transitions
summary: The vertex model is widely used to describe the mechanics of epithelial tissues, but its conventional formulation assumes that all cells remain tightly packed and always share edges with their neighbors, making it difficult to represent local detachment or gap formation. Here, we propose a minimal extension of the vertex model that enables cell detachment by introducing a new topological transformation, T2-inverse, which acts as the inverse of the classical T2 transition. When the imbalance of forces acting on a vertex, quantified by a tension metric $T$, exceeds a threshold, the T2-inverse splits the vertex into multiple vertices and creates a closed polygon that is incorporated as a pseudo-cell. This operation allows the model to represent the emergence and propagation of local detachment events. Using this framework, we simulate the stretching of a cell sheet and show that force-induced local detachments can accumulate to produce macroscopic tissue rupture. These results demonstrate that the proposed model extends the capability of the vertex model to describe tissue-level breakdown processes, including detachment and tearing, and provides a foundation for studying a broader class of epithelial mechanical phenomena.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a minimal extension of the vertex model for epithelial tissues by introducing a "T2-inverse" topological transformation that enables cell detachment and gap formation, allowing the model to simulate force-induced local detachments that accumulate into macroscopic tissue rupture under stretching.
AI.motivation: The conventional vertex model assumes cells remain tightly packed and always share edges with neighbors, which makes it impossible to represent local detachment or gap formation in epithelial tissues. This limitation prevents the model from describing tissue-level breakdown processes such as detachment and tearing.
AI.method: The authors extend the vertex model by introducing a new topological transformation called T2-inverse, which acts as the inverse of the classical T2 transition. When a tension metric T (quantifying the imbalance of forces acting on a vertex) exceeds a threshold, the T2-inverse splits the vertex into multiple vertices and creates a closed polygon that is incorporated as a pseudo-cell, enabling the representation of local detachment and gap formation.
AI.result: Simulations of cell sheet stretching show that force-induced local detachment events can accumulate and produce macroscopic tissue rupture, demonstrating the model's capability to describe tissue-level breakdown.
AI.conclusion: The proposed extended vertex model successfully captures detachment and tearing phenomena in epithelial tissues and provides a foundation for studying a broader class of epithelial mechanical phenomena beyond the tightly packed regime.

title: High-Order Triadic Functional Connectivity in the Brain and Beyond
summary: Here, we report high-order functional network connectivity as a promising way for studying the brain connectome. Traditional functional connectivity approaches capture only pairwise relationships between brain regions, overlooking complex multivariate dependencies that underlie cognition and behavior. First, we demonstrated that high-order interactions capture more information and can distinguish between resting-state and task-state brain activity. Second, we introduce a matrix-based entropy-functional method for estimating triadic interactions, which are statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions, and apply it to large-scale functional brain networks. The resulting triadic networks revealed distinct community patterns that complement those observed in traditional pairwise functional connectivity analyses and simultaneously capture additional connection information. Despite the potential combinatorial explosion of triadic configurations, the networks exhibited constrained and hierarchical structures that allowed computation and interpretation. These findings position triadic connectivity as a promising next-step functional connectivity framework for probing brain network organization and high-order neural interactions, while also highlighting key biological and technical challenges that require careful consideration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes high-order functional network connectivity, specifically triadic (three-way) interactions, as a novel framework for studying brain connectomes. Using a matrix-based entropy-functional method, the authors estimate statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions, showing that triadic networks capture additional information beyond traditional pairwise functional connectivity and reveal distinct, hierarchically organized community patterns that distinguish between resting and task states.
AI.motivation: Traditional functional connectivity methods only capture pairwise relationships between brain regions, overlooking the complex multivariate dependencies that likely underlie cognition and behavior. The authors aim to address this limitation by proposing high-order interactions as a more informative framework for studying brain network organization.
AI.method: The authors first demonstrate that high-order interactions capture more information than pairwise approaches and can distinguish resting-state from task-state brain activity. They then introduce a matrix-based entropy-functional method for estimating triadic interactions (statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions) and apply it to large-scale functional brain networks to construct triadic connectivity networks.
AI.result: The resulting triadic networks revealed distinct community patterns that complement traditional pairwise functional connectivity analyses while capturing additional connection information. Despite the combinatorial explosion of possible triadic configurations, the networks exhibited constrained, hierarchical structures that enabled computation and interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Triadic connectivity represents a promising next-step functional connectivity framework for probing brain network organization and high-order neural interactions, though key biological and technical challenges remain that require careful consideration.

title: Axonal delay dispersion decides whether a neuron detects an event or a sequence, and predicts cortical column diameter
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, under preparation for PLOS Computational Biology
summary: Cortical neurons fire sparsely -- often fewer than one spike per sensory window -- making rate coding insufficient and temporal coding a necessity. That conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony is long established. What governs which class of temporal feature a neuron detects -- one volley of coincident input, or two in a particular order -- has not been examined. We propose a delay-signature framework in which the axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch constitute a physical key: only input sequences whose spike-time differences the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection, via calcium plateau thresholds, converts that synchrony into an all-or-none output. In simulations of an integrator-neuron model we report three results. First, a single physical scalar -- the dispersion of the delay set -- moves a population from event detection to order-selective sequence detection. The transition is emergent under random delays and connectivity: at narrow dispersion sequence detectors do not exist, and the dispersion at which they overtake event detectors tracks the inter-event interval with a slope statistically indistinguishable from one. This maps a computational distinction onto the anatomical one between myelinated and unmyelinated projections, making myelination a switch on what a neuron computes, not only a regulator of speed. Second, the same dispersion sets the code's limits: it bounds the longest codable interval and fixes an absolute timing tolerance of about a millisecond, with slowing better tolerated than speeding. Third, that millisecond window and horizontal conduction velocity together predict cortical column diameter, and the two areas with direct measurements fall where the relation puts them. One anatomically measurable parameter thus sets what a neuron detects and the limits of what it can represent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a "delay-signature framework" proposing that axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch act as a physical key determining which temporal features cortical neurons detect. Simulations show a single scalar—dispersion of delay sets—controls whether neurons perform event detection or order-selective sequence detection, with myelination acting as a computational switch. The framework also explains coding limits (millisecond timing tolerance) and predicts cortical column diameter from conduction velocity.
AI.motivation: Cortical neurons fire sparsely, making rate coding insufficient and temporal coding necessary. While it is established that conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony, what determines which temporal feature a neuron detects (single coincident volley vs. ordered sequence) has not been examined.
AI.method: The authors propose a delay-signature framework where axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch constitute a physical key—only input sequences whose spike-time differences are compensated by delays arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection via calcium plateau thresholds converts synchrony into output. They use simulations of an integrator-neuron model to test whether dispersion of the delay set controls detection behavior.
AI.result: Three results: (1) Delay dispersion moves a population from event detection to order-selective sequence detection, mapping onto the anatomical distinction between myelinated and unmyelinated projections—making myelination a computational switch. (2) The same dispersion sets coding limits: bounds longest codable interval, fixes ~1ms timing tolerance with asymmetric tolerance (slowing better tolerated than speeding). (3) The millisecond window and conduction velocity predict cortical column diameter, matching direct measurements.
AI.conclusion: One anatomically measurable parameter (delay dispersion) simultaneously determines what a neuron detects, the limits of what it can represent, and predicts structural features of cortex. Myelination is reframed as a switch controlling the computational class of a neuron, not merely a speed regulator.

title: Enumerating Chemical Structures, Stereoisomers, and Stereogenic Units with Analytic Combinatorics
comment: Submitted to J. Math. Chem. 27 pages, 7 figures
summary: The enumeration of chemical structures traditionally relies on graph- and group-theoretic techniques, including Pólya theory, in order to account for stereochemical symmetries. These methods require bespoke derivations and methods for each molecular family of interest, and quickly become very intricate for nontrivial classes. In this work, we demonstrate that analytic combinatorics provides a unifying, highly extensible, and relatively simple framework for enumeration problems. Using the symbolic method, we show that classical counting problems, such as the enumeration of acyclic alkanes and other hydrocarbon families, can be naturally solved via concise combinatorial specifications of the class of interest. We first demonstrate the simplicity of this approach by replicating existing results in this framework, requiring significantly less work than previously necessary, and then extend these ideas to more complex problems, counting broader classes of molecules accounting for both tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, counting the distribution of stereogenic units, and enumerating achiral and meso compounds. All results are made reproducible through CombOL, our open-source software package which automates the translation of combinatorial specifications into generating functions using the symbolic method, and performs both univariate and multivariate enumeration.

AI.tldr: This paper presents analytic combinatorics as a unifying, extensible framework for enumerating chemical structures, replacing traditional graph/group-theoretic methods like Pólya theory. Using the symbolic method, the authors solve classical problems (e.g., acyclic alkane enumeration) more easily and extend to complex cases including tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral/meso compounds. Results are reproducible via CombOL, an open-source software package.
AI.motivation: Traditional enumeration methods based on graph theory and group theory (e.g., Pólya theory) require bespoke derivations for each molecular family, become highly intricate for nontrivial classes, and lack a unified approach.
AI.method: The authors apply analytic combinatorics and the symbolic method to construct concise combinatorial specifications of molecular classes, which are then translated into generating functions. This framework is implemented in CombOL, an open-source tool that automates this translation for both univariate and multivariate enumeration.
AI.result: The framework replicates known results (e.g., acyclic alkane enumeration) with significantly less effort than prior methods, and extends to more complex problems including broader molecule classes with tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral and meso compound enumeration.
AI.conclusion: Analytic combinatorics provides a simpler, unifying, and highly extensible framework for chemical enumeration, with all results made reproducible through the open-source CombOL software package.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
summary: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

AI.tldr: A unified computational framework for tensor-based morphometry that combines surface modeling, diffusion smoothing via Laplace-Beltrami operator, and statistical analysis to localize cortical surface shape differences between clinical groups from MRI data.
AI.motivation: Cortical surface shape differences (local surface area and curvature) between clinical groups are unlikely to be uniform across the cortex, yet existing methods lack a coherent unified mathematical framework combining surface modeling, smoothing, and statistical analysis to localize regions of most rapid structural differences.
AI.method: Combines surface modeling of the 2D cortical sheet with diffusion smoothing based on explicit Laplace-Beltrami operator estimation to increase signal-to-noise ratio, applied to surface metrics within a unified tensor-based morphometry framework for statistical group comparison.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated by localizing cortical regions of gray matter tissue growth and loss in longitudinally collected brain images from a group of children.
AI.conclusion: The unified tensor-based surface morphometry framework effectively localizes regional cortical shape differences, as illustrated by detecting gray matter growth and loss patterns in pediatric longitudinal data.

title: Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus
summary: Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an epidemiological/viral model to understand LLM adoption, distinguishing uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, showing that social transmission dynamics can create tipping points, technological lock-in, and runaway shifts toward persistent dependence with cognitive competence loss—but also identifying conditions for "cognitive immunization" via reduced transmission and increased reversibility.
AI.motivation: LLMs are rapidly reshaping human culture and information practices, yet there is no formal framework for understanding how their adoption spreads and potentially leads to collective dependence with cognitive consequences.
AI.method: The authors model transitions among three user states (uncoupled, coupled, persistently dependent) using a framework that incorporates social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement to analyze population-level adoption dynamics.
AI.result: The model reveals tipping points and technological lock-in, demonstrating that once a critical adoption threshold is crossed, runaway dynamics can trigger rapid population shifts toward persistent dependence and abrupt cognitive competence losses. The framework also identifies conditions for cognitive immunization through reduced transmission and enhanced reversibility.
AI.conclusion: LLM adoption involves nonlinear collective transitions with important implications for cognitive autonomy, and interventions targeting transmission and reversibility may protect against persistent dependence.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SimpleDesign is a single-stage, end-to-end multi-modal protein design model trained directly in data space using a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that jointly handles sequence and structure generation without the need for multi-stage latent-space training.
AI.motivation: Existing protein co-design models rely on multi-stage training (first tokenizing data into latent representations via autoencoders, then training a generative model in latent space). The authors hypothesize this multi-stage training is not necessary for performant co-design models.
AI.method: SimpleDesign uses a single-stage end-to-end objective combining discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. It employs a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that enables modality-specific processing while maintaining global self-attention over both sequence and structure modalities. The model is trained on over 2M sequence-structure pairs.
AI.result: SimpleDesign achieves strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage latent-space training is not necessary for effective multi-modal protein design; a single-stage approach trained directly in data space with an appropriate architecture can achieve competitive results.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: RNN Maxent replaces the fixed feature dictionary in Maxent with a GRU neural network trained end-to-end, preserving Maxent's presence-only foundations while learning nonlinear temporal relationships from environmental time-series data. Applied to Desert Locust habitat mapping with 50-day environmental sequences, it outperforms standard Maxent (AUC 0.862 vs 0.792; F1 0.671 vs 0.590).
AI.motivation: Standard Maxent relies on linear combinations of hand-chosen feature transforms, which cannot capture the nonlinear and temporal relationships in ecological monitoring data. Time-series covariates (precipitation, soil moisture, vegetation) are flattened into independent features, discarding the sequential structure that carries critical signal for species like the Desert Locust whose breeding is coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions.
AI.method: RNN Maxent replaces Maxent's fixed feature dictionary with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) neural network, trained end-to-end via backpropagation. The model preserves Maxent's presence-only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, but the nonlinearity is learned from data. Applied using 50-day environmental time series (ERA5 Land, MODIS, Sentinel 3) with a 7-day gap between covariates and presence records for forecasting behavior.
AI.result: RNN Maxent improves performance over standard Maxent across metrics: ROC AUC 0.862 (std 0.036) vs 0.792, and F1 0.671 (std 0.056) vs 0.590, demonstrating the benefit of learning temporal structure in species distribution modeling.
AI.conclusion: Learning nonlinear temporal relationships from data, rather than relying on fixed feature transforms, significantly improves species distribution modeling for environmentally dynamic pests like the Desert Locust, offering better forecasting of suitable habitat.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that a simple deterministic artificial agent equipped with an affective system that experiences felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs can display hedonic place preference behavior—typically associated with feelings in biological creatures—challenging assumptions about the link between such behavior and subjective experience, with implications for understanding consciousness and free will.
AI.motivation: Scientists interpret hedonic place preference behavior in creatures (attraction to pleasure-producing but nutritionless substances like cocaine or morphine) as evidence of feelings, since such attraction seems inexplicable by unconscious instinct. The authors question this assumption by exploring whether this behavior can arise in a purely deterministic artificial system.
AI.method: The authors construct a simple artificial agent that instantiates key attributes of an affective system—specifically felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs relative to environmental resources. The agent engages in an apparently subjective form of information processing while remaining fully deterministic, and they observe whether it exhibits hedonic place preference behavior.
AI.result: The deterministic artificial agent, through its affective information processing architecture, successfully displays hedonic place preference behavior similar to biological creatures—achieving the apparent subjective experience through entirely deterministic mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The authors outline implications for understanding the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will, suggesting that hedonic place preference behavior alone may not be sufficient evidence of genuine subjective feelings, and that such apparently subjective behaviors can emerge from wholly deterministic systems.

title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
summary: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs), and ask whether this failure mode can be addressed by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective. Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the intervention in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, prospective variants match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every model and configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF reaches 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. These results identify RQFs as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate and prospective-input coding as an input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters (a special case of diagonal state-space models), and proposes a prospective-input correction for each layer's bottom-up input to address depth-dependent gradient attenuation in deep continuous-time recurrent networks. The intervention mitigates temporal gradient truncation issues and improves or matches performance across RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs.
AI.motivation: Temporal integration gives recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors, creating a failure mode for deep continuous-time recurrent networks. The authors ask whether making each layer's bottom-up input prospective can address this issue.
AI.method: Starting from an energy model, the authors derive RQF dynamics, showing each RQF is a band-pass filter with learnable tuning frequency and bandwidth. They make bottom-up inputs prospective via a parameter-free two-tap update that preserves the recurrent transition and parallel scan, extending this correction to general diagonal SSMs. This mitigates gradient attenuation under spatial-only backpropagation.
AI.result: Prospective variants match or outperform non-prospective controls across all models/configurations under full BPTT. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters, and a width-64 six-layer RQF achieves 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task.
AI.conclusion: RQFs are identified as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate, and prospective-input coding serves as an input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks.
